props.title: Gentleman's Agreement
props.initialSlug: Reporter poses as Jewish to expose antisemitism

sections.content: Gentleman's Agreement (1947) broke new ground as one of Hollywood's first major confrontations with antisemitism. Gregory Peck plays a journalist who poses as Jewish to expose discrimination, delivering a powerful indictment of polite society's casual bigotry. The film shares DNA with other bold social problem films of its era like Crossfire (1947) and The Best Years of Our Lives (1946), but goes further by indicting not just obvious bigots but the "nice people" who enable discrimination through their silence and compliance. Director Elia Kazan, fresh off his Broadway success, brings a raw theatrical energy that would later define classics like On the Waterfront (1954).

sections.content: The film's release came at a crucial moment, as Hollywood finally began addressing prejudice head-on after WWII. While The House I Live In (1945) with Frank Sinatra had touched on religious tolerance, and Till the End of Time (1946) explored veteran discrimination, Gentleman's Agreement went deeper by showing how antisemitism thrived in upper-class social circles. The film won Best Picture, Director, and Supporting Actress for Celeste Holm, though some critics felt it didn't go far enough in its indictment of systemic racism. SUBHEAD: Impact and Legacy

The success of Gentleman's Agreement opened doors for more films tackling prejudice, like Pinky (1949) and Home of the Brave (1949). But it also marked a turning point in how Hollywood approached "message pictures." Rather than melodramatic treatments like The House I Live In (1945), films began taking a more naturalistic approach to social issues. This influence can be traced through later works like The Defiant Ones (1958) and Guess Who's Coming to Dinner (1967), showing how mainstream cinema could tackle discrimination while still delivering compelling drama.
